procedural_history.originating_court: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Punjab (State Commission)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 20.02.2019, passed by the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi (NCDRC) in First Appeal No. 207/2015, by which the NCDRC set aside the order passed by the State Commission and modified it to the extent that the insurance company shall be liable to pay only Rs. 12,60,000/- instead of Rs. 29,17,500/-.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Insurance company appealed the order of the State Commission to the NCDRC. The NCDRC allowed the appeal and modified the order of the State Commission, awarding Rs. 12,60,000/- instead of Rs. 29,17,500/-.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The original complainant (M/S Oswal Plastic Industries) felt aggrieved and dissatisfied with the NCDRC's judgment and order and preferred an appeal to the Supreme Court.

decision.appeal_result: Appeal allowed. The impugned judgment and order passed by the NCDRC is hereby quashed and set aside. The order passed by the State Commission is hereby restored.
directions: The complainant shall be entitled to Rs. 29,17,500/- being the reinstatement value with interest @ 7% from the date of order of the State Commission.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complainant is entitled to the reinstatement value or the depreciated value for the damaged plant and machinery under the terms of the insurance policy?

facts: The complainant's plant and machinery, insured under a Fire & Perils policy, were damaged in a fire.
A surveyor appointed by the insurance company assessed the loss at Rs. 29,17,500 on a 'reinstatement value' basis and Rs. 12,60,000 on a 'depreciated value' basis.
The State Commission awarded the complainant the reinstatement value (Rs. 29,17,500).
On appeal, the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) set aside the State Commission's order and awarded the lower depreciated value (Rs. 12,60,000).
The complainant then appealed the NCDRC's decision to the Supreme Court.
law: The decision hinged on the interpretation of Clause 9 of Section 2 of the insurance policy.
1. It gives the insurance company the option to physically reinstate or replace the damaged property instead of paying the cash value of the loss.

2. If the company is unable to reinstate or repair the property (due to regulations 'or otherwise'), it is liable to pay 'such sum as would be requisite to reinstate or repair such property if the same could lawfully be reinstated to its former condition.'
application: The Supreme Court determined that the case fell under the second part of Clause 9, as the insurance company was unable to physically reinstate or repair the damaged property.
The Court interpreted the phrase 'pay such sum as would be requisite to reinstate or repair' to mean the reinstatement value, not the depreciated value.
It held that the surveyor's report, which calculated the reinstatement value at Rs. 29,17,500, was the relevant evidence to determine this sum.
The Court found that the NCDRC had 'mis-interpreted and mis-read' Clause 9 and had 'seriously erred' in holding that the insurance company was only liable for the depreciated value.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that, according to the terms of Clause 9 of the insurance policy, the complainant was entitled to the reinstatement value of the damaged machinery. Consequently, the Court set aside the NCDRC's order and restored the State Commission's original order awarding the complainant Rs. 29,17,500.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the complainant is entitled to the reinstatement value or the depreciated value for the damaged plant and machinery under the terms of the insurance policy?
appellant_arguments: The complainant purchased new machinery to replace the ones destroyed in the fire, justifying the reinstatement value of Rs. 29,17,500/- awarded by the State Commission, which was based on the surveyor's report.
Clause 9 of Section 2 of the insurance policy entitles the complainant to the reinstatement value. The NCDRC misinterpreted this clause.

Clause 9 merely gives the insurance company an option to reinstate or replace the property. Since the company did not exercise this option, the clause was not applicable in the manner interpreted by the NCDRC.

Citing the case of Canara Bank Vs. United India Insurance Company Limited, it was argued that insurance policy provisions should be interpreted broadly, and any ambiguity must be resolved in favor of the insured to meet the reasonable expectations of the parties.
respondent_arguments: The NCDRC correctly interpreted Clause 9 of the insurance policy and did not err in awarding the depreciated value instead of the reinstatement value.
The insured goods were to be replaced on an 'as is basis,' meaning an old machine should be replaced by an old machine.

Since neither party actually reinstated the machinery, the monetary compensation should be the value of an equivalent old machine, which can only be calculated by deducting depreciation from the current value of new machinery.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under an insurance policy clause providing that if the insurer is unable to reinstate or repair damaged property, it shall be liable to pay the sum requisite to reinstate or repair such property to its former condition, the insured is entitled to the reinstatement value of the property, not its depreciated value.
obiter: The report of a surveyor is relevant evidence to consider the sum required to reinstate or repair insured property.

Provisions of an insurance policy must be read and interpreted to give effect to the reasonable expectations of all parties, with coverage provisions interpreted broadly and any ambiguity resolved in favor of the insured.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's decision rests on a direct interpretation of the second part of Clause 9 of the insurance policy. It found that this clause specifically addresses situations where the insurance company is unable to reinstate or repair the damaged property. In such an eventuality, the policy obligates the company to pay the sum that would be necessary to reinstate or repair the property to its former condition. Therefore, the complainant is entitled to the reinstatement value, not the depreciated value, and the surveyor's report is the relevant evidence for determining this amount.
legal_tests_applied: Interpretation of contractual terms within an insurance policy, specifically focusing on the plain meaning and structure of the reinstatement clause (Clause 9, Section 2).
why_respondent_won: The court interpreted the second part of Clause 9 of Section 2 of the policy, which states, 'If in any case the Company shall be unable to reinstate or repair the property hereby insured... the Company shall, in every such case, only be liable to pay such sum as would be requisite to reinstate or repair such property if the same could lawfully be reinstated to its former condition.'
The court determined that the present case fell under this 'second eventuality,' where the insurance company was unable to reinstate or repair the property.
Based on this clause, the court concluded that the insurance company is liable to pay the sum 'requisite to reinstate or repair,' which corresponds to the reinstatement value.

The court held that the surveyor's report, which assessed the loss on a reinstatement value basis at Rs. 29,17,500/-, is the relevant evidence to determine the sum required to reinstate or repair the property.

The court found that the NCDRC had 'mis-interpreted and mis-read the Clause 9' and 'seriously erred in observing and holding that the insurance company shall be liable to pay the depreciated value only and not the reinstatement value.'
